flawed_step: The claim assumes the MST is unique, or that both algorithms break ties the same way. When edges have equal weights, neither holds, so the two algorithms can legally output different trees.
counterexample:
Graph: a triangle with vertices a, b, c and edges ab, bc, ca, each of weight 1. It is connected, and every spanning tree has 2 edges and weight 2, so every spanning tree is an MST.
Kruskal run: sort the tied edges as ab, bc, ca. Take ab (it joins {a} and {b}). Take bc (it joins {a,b} and {c}). Reject ca (it would make a cycle). Output: {ab, bc}.
Prim run: start at a. The crossing edges are ab and ac, both weight 1; break the tie by choosing ac, so the tree is {a,c}. The crossing edges are now ab and cb, both weight 1; break the tie by choosing ab, so the tree is {a,b,c}. Output: {ac, ab}.
The edge sets {ab, bc} and {ab, ac} are different, and both are MSTs of weight 2.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. In a triangle whose three edges all have weight 1, a legal Kruskal run outputs {ab, bc}. A legal Prim run starting at a outputs {ab, ac}. Both are minimum spanning trees of weight 2, but they are different edge sets. The two algorithms are only guaranteed to agree when the MST is unique, for example when all edge weights are distinct.
